371.quote_or_event: “Make the effort, and you shall live; practicing it, you shall enjoy peace.”
371.explanation: In the Gujri ki Vaar Guru Arjan urges udam, steady effort on the path of the Name, and promises that such effort brings true life and peace.
371.tie_back: The Kural says a fortune bent on giving shows itself as tireless effort; Guru Arjan likewise treats unflagging effort as the way blessings arrive, though he presents it as a duty to take up rather than a sign that fortune has already decided.
371.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 522, Raag Gujri (Gujri ki Vaar, salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
371._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the verse praises spiritual effort and does not say that destiny produces effort or laziness, which is the Kural's actual claim.

372.quote_or_event: “Those, whom the Creator Lord would destroy - first He strips them of virtue.”
372.explanation: In a hymn of the Babarvani, reflecting on the ruin of the rich and powerful in Babar's invasion, Guru Nanak observes that before the Creator brings someone down, He first takes away their goodness and judgement.
372.tie_back: The Kural says a fate of loss makes even the clever act foolishly; Guru Nanak names the same pattern, in which ruin begins by stripping a person of the qualities that would have saved them.
372.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
372._accuracy_note: Strong fit for the first half of the couplet; Gurbani speaks of virtue rather than intelligence and the line does not cover the second half, that good fortune widens understanding.

373.quote_or_event: “You may read and read loads of books; you may read and study vast multitudes of books.” … “O Nanak, only one thing is of any account: everything else is useless babbling and idle talk in ego.”
373.explanation: In Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak says that no quantity of reading counts in the end; only one thing, the Lord's Name and praise, is of account, and the rest is ego talking.
373.tie_back: The Kural says that however many subtle books one studies, only the understanding truly one's own prevails; Guru Nanak likewise ranks bookish learning below the one thing that really counts.
373.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 467, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
373._accuracy_note: Two verified lines from the same salok, with the lines between them left out; the shared point is that book learning is subordinate, but for Guru Nanak what counts is the Name, not an understanding allotted by fate.

374.quote_or_event: “By His Command, some are high and some are low; by His Written Command, pain and pleasure are obtained.”
374.explanation: In the second pauri of Japji Guru Nanak teaches that hukam, the divine order, assigns people different stations and different shares of pain and pleasure.
374.tie_back: The Kural observes that fate deals out wealth and wisdom on two separate tracks; Japji likewise sees people's unequal portions as handed out by the one divine order rather than earned by merit alone.
374.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji Sahib, Pauri 2, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
374._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: hukam explains unequal portions in general, but the verse does not separate wealth from wisdom as the Kural does.

375.quote_or_event: “Suffering is the medicine, and pleasure the disease, because where there is pleasure, there is no desire for God.”
375.explanation: In Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak turns the usual valuation upside down: hardship heals by turning the mind to God, while comfort sickens by making one forget Him.
375.tie_back: The Kural says fate can turn every favourable circumstance unfavourable and every unfavourable one favourable; Guru Nanak shows the same reversal, with good fortune becoming harmful and misfortune becoming a cure.
375.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 469, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
375._accuracy_note: Next-best: the reversal of good and bad is shared, but Guru Nanak speaks of spiritual benefit, whereas the Kural concerns success and failure in gaining wealth.

376.quote_or_event: “He obtains ten things, and puts them behind him; for the sake of one thing withheld, he forfeits his faith. But what if that one thing were not given, and the ten were taken away? Then, what could the fool say or do?”
376.explanation: In Sukhmani Guru Arjan reminds the ungrateful person that everything they hold was given by God and can be taken back at will, and that nothing they do can then keep it.
376.tie_back: The Kural says what is not one's allotted share cannot be kept however carefully it is guarded; Guru Arjan likewise teaches that what the Giver withholds or takes back cannot be held on to.
376.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 268, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib (Ashtpadi 5), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
376._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on gifts that cannot be held against the Giver's will; Sukhmani's own aim is gratitude, and it does not cover the Kural's other half, that what is one's own cannot be thrown away.

377.quote_or_event: “Why, O mind, do you plot and plan, when the Dear Lord Himself provides for your care? From rocks and stones He created living beings; He places their nourishment before them.”
377.explanation: In this hymn, recited daily in the evening prayer So Dar (Rehras), Guru Arjan tells the anxious mind that sustenance (rizak) is set out by God for every creature, even those born inside rock.
377.tie_back: The Kural says even those who amass crores enjoy only what the Ordainer has apportioned; Guru Arjan likewise teaches that each creature's portion is arranged by the Lord, so scheming adds nothing to it.
377.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 10, So Dar (Rehras), Raag Gujri, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
377._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both see one's portion as divinely apportioned, but Guru Arjan stresses God's provision and trust, not the limit on enjoying great wealth.

378.quote_or_event: “So many endure distress, deprivation and constant abuse. Even these are Your Gifts, O Great Giver!”
378.explanation: In the twenty-fifth pauri of Japji Guru Nanak says that the hunger and suffering many people endure are also part of what the Giver hands out.
378.tie_back: The Kural, in its most debated couplet, says the destitute would renounce the world if fate did not make them live through their allotted sufferings; Japji also sees such suffering as allotted, though as a gift to be accepted rather than a debt fate collects.
378.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 5, Japji Sahib, Pauri 25, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
378._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Japji shares the idea of allotted suffering, but nothing in it matches the Kural's point about the poor and renunciation, and Sikhism rejects renunciation in favour of the householder life.

379.quote_or_event: “That man, who in the midst of pain, does not feel pain, who is not affected by pleasure, affection or fear, and who looks alike upon gold and dust;”
379.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur describes the person in whom God dwells as one who is not shaken by pain and not carried away by pleasure, holding gold and dust alike.
379.tie_back: The Kural asks why one who welcomes good fortune should grieve at misfortune, since both come from the same source; Guru Tegh Bahadur portrays the person who meets pleasure and pain with exactly that evenness.
379.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 633, Raag Sorath, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
379._accuracy_note: Strong fit on equanimity toward good and bad fortune; the hymn grounds it in God's presence rather than in the Kural's argument that both come from the same fate.

380.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, whatever I wish for does not happen. What can I accomplish by merely thinking? The Lord does whatever He wishes; it is not up to me at all.”
380.explanation: In a salok preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib, Bhagat Kabir admits that his own plans count for nothing, because the Lord carries out His own will, which is often beyond what one has even imagined.
380.tie_back: The Kural closes the Book of Virtue by asking what is mightier than fate, which arrives first even when one plans another way; Kabir likewise says the Lord's will prevails over whatever we plan.
380.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1376, Salok Bhagat Kabir 219 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
380._accuracy_note: Near match on human planning being overruled; Gurbani attributes this to a personal Lord's will (hukam) rather than to impersonal fate.
